blocks.content: 1. Problem Statement

blocks.text:
Design Netflix: a global, subscription based video streaming platform where a catalog of movies and TV shows can be uploaded once by content operations, encoded into many different quality levels, and then streamed smoothly to hundreds of millions of viewers on phones, laptops, game consoles, and televisions, on every kind of network connection from gigabit fiber to a single flaky bar of cellular signal on a subway train.

It helps to say up front what this problem is really testing. It is not really a database design question, and it is not really a video codec question either. It is a question about asymmetric systems: a small, comparatively simple amount of work happens once per title when it is uploaded and encoded, and then an almost unimaginably large amount of work happens over and over again every time someone presses play. Almost every interesting decision in this design falls out of taking that asymmetry seriously.

At a very high level, the system has two halves that barely resemble each other. One half is a content pipeline: a studio or licensing partner uploads a single high quality master file, and that file is asynchronously chewed through a transcoding pipeline that produces a whole ladder of renditions, from a tiny 240p stream for a weak connection up through 4K for a fast one, each in more than one codec. The other half is a playback system: hundreds of millions of client devices asking, from every corner of the planet, for tiny few-second chunks of that already-encoded video, chosen moment to moment to match whatever their network happens to be doing right now. Everything from here on is about designing both halves well, and, just as importantly, keeping them from getting in each other's way.

3. Non-Functional Requirements

3.1 Scalability

blocks.text: The system needs to comfortably support on the order of hundreds of millions of subscribers, tens of millions of concurrent streams during peak hours, and a catalog that keeps growing every week. Crucially, the playback path and the encoding path need to scale independently of each other, since they grow for completely different reasons and at completely different rates.

3.2 Availability

blocks.text: A user who taps play and gets an error, or a spinner that never resolves, is a user who is one tap away from opening a competitor's app instead. Playback availability needs to be extremely high, effectively always on, even while individual data centers, edge caches, or backend services are having a bad day somewhere in the world.

3.3 Reliability

blocks.text: Once a title has been successfully encoded, it needs to stay playable indefinitely, or until it is deliberately removed for a licensing reason. A watch position, once saved, should not quietly vanish and force a viewer to hunt for where they left off. Reliability here is less about any single request succeeding and more about state not getting silently lost over time.

3.4 Performance

blocks.text: Two numbers matter more than almost anything else: how long it takes from tapping play to the first frame appearing, and how often playback has to pause to rebuffer. Both should be small enough that most viewers never consciously notice them at all.

3.5 Fault Tolerance and Consistency

blocks.text: When something in the system is unhealthy, an edge cache node down, a region degraded, a recommendation service slow, the system should degrade gracefully rather than fail outright. A slightly stale row of recommendations, or a watch position that is a few seconds behind reality, is a completely acceptable price to pay for keeping the video itself flowing without interruption.

3.6 Security

blocks.text: Video content is expensive, licensed intellectual property, and studios require real assurances that it cannot simply be downloaded and redistributed. Every stream needs to be delivered only to authenticated, authorized sessions, encrypted in transit, and protected by content protection technology that a casual attacker cannot trivially bypass.

items: Scale: roughly 260 million paying subscribers worldwide, with about 100 million daily active viewers.
Watch time: an active viewer streams for roughly 2 hours on an average day.
Catalog size: roughly 50,000 individually playable video assets, counting both movies and individual TV episodes, averaging about 45 minutes of runtime each.

Rendition ladder: every asset is encoded at 6 resolutions, 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, and 4K, in 2 codec families, one for broad device compatibility and one modern, more efficient codec, for 12 renditions total per asset.
Read to write ratio on the data plane: a single upload turns into millions of playback views over a title's lifetime, an extremely read heavy system on the video bytes themselves.
Write frequency on watch position: the opposite pattern, a tiny record updated extremely often for every single active viewer.
Global footprint: traffic is spread across every populated continent and time zone, which smooths some peaks but concentrates others around regional prime time viewing hours.

5.1 Business and licensing constraints

blocks.text: Content availability is not uniform. A title licensed for streaming in one country may be completely unavailable in another, and licensing windows expire, meaning a title that was playable yesterday may need to disappear from a region today. The catalog and playback authorization layers both need to treat "is this title available to this viewer, right now" as a first class question, not an afterthought bolted on later.

6.1 Concurrency and bandwidth

blocks.text: Start with the daily active number from Section 5: 100 million viewers, each streaming for about 2 hours a day on average. That works out to 100,000,000 * 2, or 200 million user-hours of playback spread across a single day. If that were perfectly even across all 24 hours, average concurrency would be a modest 200,000,000 / 24, a little over 8 million simultaneous streams. Viewing is not even, though, it concentrates heavily around evening hours in every region, so a realistic peak factor of roughly 2.5x on top of that average lands peak concurrency at approximately 20 million simultaneous streams worldwide.

blocks.text: Now multiply that by bandwidth per stream. Netflix serves a mix of resolutions, mostly clustered around standard and high definition rather than 4K, so a reasonable blended average is about 5 Mbps per stream. Multiply it out: 20,000,000 streams * 5 Mbps comes out to 100 terabits per second of playback bandwidth at peak, globally. That number alone is the entire justification for everything in Section 14: no single data center, or even a modest number of data centers, can push 100 Tbps directly to consumer devices. The only way this works is if the overwhelming majority of that bandwidth is served from caches sitting physically inside or next to the ISPs that carry the last mile, not from Netflix's own infrastructure at all.

blocks.text: Take the rendition ladder from Section 5: 6 resolutions across 2 codec families, 12 renditions per asset. Summing typical bitrates across the resolution ladder, roughly 300 kbps at 240p up through roughly 16 Mbps at 4K, the full ladder for one codec family adds up to about 25 Mbps of combined bitrate across all six resolutions. The second, more efficient codec family achieves similar visual quality at roughly half the bitrate, adding about 12.5 Mbps more. Combined across all 12 renditions, that is roughly 37.5 Mbps of aggregate encoded bitrate per minute of source content, which works out to about 37,500 kbps / 8, or a little under 5 megabytes, of combined storage per second of runtime across every rendition put together.

https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208123242-19106265.png
blocks.alt: One hundred million daily viewers, each sending a watch position heartbeat roughly every ten seconds during playback, adds up to hundreds of thousands of writes every second

blocks.text: This is the part of the system that looks tiny and turns out to be enormous. If a client sends a watch position update roughly every 10 seconds during active playback, and the 100 million daily active viewers collectively generate the 200 million user-hours of playback computed above, that is 200,000,000 * 3600 seconds of playback per day, or 720 billion device-seconds. Divide by a 10 second heartbeat interval and that is 72 billion watch position writes per day. Spread evenly across 86,400 seconds in a day, that averages out to roughly 72,000,000,000 / 86,400, or about 833,000 writes per second, sustained, around the clock, with peak hours pushing that comfortably past a million writes a second. Every one of those writes is tiny, a user id, a title id, a position, and a timestamp, but the sheer frequency means this unglamorous little service needs the write throughput characteristics of a serious distributed key-value store, not an afterthought bolted onto the catalog database.

blocks.text: Any estimate handed to an interviewer should survive being wrong by a large factor, because real projections usually are. If peak concurrency were actually 40 million instead of 20 million, bandwidth needs double to roughly 200 Tbps, which strengthens rather than weakens the case for CDN edge caching. The watch position write rate is the number most worth stress testing, because a distributed key-value store handling a few million writes a second at global scale is achievable but is not a decision to make lightly, and it drives real sizing conversations in Section 18.

7. High-Level Architecture

blocks.text: This is the picture that everything else in this document zooms into. The single most important idea in the entire design sits right here: this system is really two systems wearing one name. One is a control plane, a comparatively small, low bandwidth collection of services that answer questions like who is this user, what can they watch, and what should we recommend. The other is a data plane, an enormous, high bandwidth pipeline that turns uploaded video into cached bytes and pushes those bytes to devices. The control plane makes decisions. The data plane moves the actual video. They scale for completely different reasons, they fail in completely different ways, and treating them as one undifferentiated blob of "the backend" is the single most common mistake a candidate can make on this problem.

7.1 The control plane

This half of the system is relatively modest in raw bandwidth terms, its job is answering questions quickly and correctly, not moving gigabytes. It looks, and largely behaves, like a fairly conventional set of horizontally scaled microservices sitting in front of a handful of databases, the kind of architecture that would not look out of place in Section 7 of almost any other system design document.

blocks.text: 7.2 The data plane, and the transcoding pipeline that feeds it
blocks.content: 7.2 The data plane, and the transcoding pipeline that feeds it
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208068401-807199876.png
blocks.alt: A raw master file is validated, chunked, and fanned out to a worker fleet that produces every rendition in the ladder, then quality checked and packaged into segments and a manifest before landing in origin storage

blocks.text: This half of the system could not look more different. Content operations uploads a single raw master file for a title, and that file gets validated, split into chunks that can be encoded in parallel, and fanned out across a large fleet of transcoding workers. Each worker handles one rendition of one chunk at a time, so a single title's encode job might run as hundreds of small parallel tasks rather than one long sequential one. This is genuinely heavy batch processing, an hour of raw 4K master footage can take a meaningful amount of compute time to fully transcode into all twelve renditions, which is exactly why it happens asynchronously, well ahead of when any viewer actually presses play, rather than on demand.

This is genuinely heavy batch processing, an hour of raw 4K master footage can take a meaningful amount of compute time to fully transcode into all twelve renditions, which is exactly why it happens asynchronously, well ahead of when any viewer actually presses play, rather than on demand.

blocks.text: Once every rendition passes an automated quality check, a packaging step chops each rendition into short segments, a few seconds each, and writes out a manifest file listing every available quality for every segment. Both the segments and the manifest land in origin storage, and for titles expected to be popular, get proactively pushed out toward CDN edges before a single viewer has asked for them.

blocks.content: 7.3 The CDN, from origin to the edge inside the ISP
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208082270-644570600.png
blocks.alt: Video requests travel from the client to an ISP edge cache first, falling back to a regional cache and finally the origin only on a cache miss

blocks.text: Here is the piece of the architecture that most candidates underweight, and it is the piece that actually makes the 100 Tbps number from Section 6 survivable at all. Netflix's real world approach, known publicly as Open Connect, places purpose built caching appliances physically inside internet service provider networks, as close to the end viewer as the network topology allows. When a device requests a video segment, that request usually never leaves the ISP's own network at all, it hits a cache sitting a few network hops away and gets served in milliseconds. Only when that edge cache does not have the segment does the request travel further, first to a larger regional cache tier, and only as a last resort all the way back to Netflix's own origin storage. The overwhelming majority of playback traffic, by design, never touches a Netflix data center.

7.4 Where the two halves meet

blocks.text: The narrow bridge between these two very different worlds is the playback authorization service. When a client wants to play a title, it talks to the control plane, which checks entitlement, picks the nearest healthy CDN edge, and hands back a signed manifest URL along with whatever content protection token is required. From that moment forward, the client talks almost exclusively to the CDN, not back to the control plane, for the rest of that viewing session, aside from the lightweight watch position heartbeat running quietly in the background. That handoff, one small control plane decision unlocking a long, high bandwidth data plane session, is the architectural hinge the whole system turns on.

13.1 Adaptive bitrate streaming, concretely
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208129953-323473456.png
blocks.alt: A single manifest file lists every available quality for every segment, letting the player choose independently for each one

blocks.text: Here is the idea that makes adaptive bitrate streaming, ABR, work, and it is worth being precise about why it beats the obvious alternative of just picking one fixed quality upfront. The video is chopped into short segments, a few seconds each, and for every single segment, every rendition produced back in Section 7.2 is available. The manifest lists all of them. Critically, the player is completely free to pick a different quality for segment six than it picked for segment five. Picking one fixed quality at the start of playback means guessing, once, about network conditions that might hold steady for two hours or might completely fall apart ninety seconds later on a subway train. Choosing per segment, continuously, based on real measured throughput and how much video is already sitting in the buffer, means the player never has to guess further ahead than a few seconds at a time.

Alice is on her morning commute, phone in hand, and taps play on an episode she started last night. Alice is on her morning commute, phone in hand, and taps play on an episode she started last night. The app calls the playback endpoint from Section 9.1, gets back a manifest URL, and the player starts pulling 1080p segments over a strong initial wifi signal near the station. blocks.text: Then her train enters a tunnel. Throughput on her cellular connection collapses almost instantly. The player is not making a single one-time decision here, it is continuously measuring two things: how fast the last few segments actually arrived, and how much buffered video is left before playback catches up to the front of what has downloaded. Both numbers start looking bad at the same time. Rather than stubbornly requesting another large 1080p segment and risking a stall, the player requests the next segment at 480p instead, a fraction of the size, and it arrives comfortably in time. Playback never stalls. A person standing next to Alice would notice the picture soften for a moment, if they noticed anything at all, they would almost certainly never see a spinner.

blocks.text: A few minutes later the train surfaces and signal recovers. The player does not jump straight back to 1080p, it steps up gradually, 480p to 720p to 1080p, confirming sustained throughput at each step before committing to the next, the same conservative logic in reverse. This entire adaptation, downward during the tunnel and back upward afterward, happens automatically, segment by segment, without Alice ever seeing a settings menu or making a single choice herself. That is the whole point of adaptive bitrate streaming: the fixed-quality alternative would have forced an impossible choice at the very start of the trip, either too high a quality that stalls constantly in the tunnel, or too low a quality that wastes Alice's excellent wifi connection for the rest of the ride.

14.3 Eviction and prewarming
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208137272-121357297.png

blocks.text: 15.1 Producer and consumer design for transcoding
blocks.content: 15.1 Producer and consumer design for transcoding
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208139718-878627939.png
blocks.alt: The ingest service produces one job per rendition into a durable queue, an autoscaled worker pool consumes them, and jobs that fail repeatedly land in a dead letter queue

blocks.text: When a new master is validated, the ingest service does not encode anything itself, it produces one job per rendition, twelve jobs per title given the ladder from Section 5, and drops them onto a durable queue. A large, independently autoscaled pool of worker instances consumes from that queue, each worker pulling one job, encoding one rendition, writing the result to origin storage, and acknowledging the job only once that write succeeds. This decoupling is exactly why a slow encode of one 4K rendition never blocks the other eleven renditions of the same title, or any other title's jobs, from making progress in parallel.

15.2 Retries and dead lettering
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208142042-676326313.png
blocks.alt: A failed job retries with exponential backoff, and only after exhausting its retry budget lands in a dead letter queue for human review

blocks.text: Encode jobs fail sometimes, a worker crashes mid-job, a chunk turns out to be malformed, a transient storage error occurs. A failed job is retried automatically with exponential backoff, spacing out retries so a systemic issue does not get hammered by every failed job retrying at once. Only after a small, fixed number of retries does a job get routed to a dead letter queue, which is deliberately treated as a signal for a human to look at, not something silently swallowed, since a rendition that never gets produced means a title stuck less than fully available.

16. Load Balancing Strategy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208149544-611816623.png
blocks.alt: Clients are routed through geo aware DNS or anycast to a regional load balancer, which distributes requests across many service instances

blocks.text: Control plane traffic is load balanced in a fairly conventional way: geo aware DNS or anycast routing sends a client to a nearby regional entry point, and a standard layer 7 load balancer spreads requests across many stateless service instances behind it. What is worth calling out is that this is genuinely a different kind of load balancing than what the CDN does. Choosing which edge cache serves a given viewer, described in Section 7.3, is really a routing and capacity decision baked into the CDN's own topology, not a traditional load balancer sitting in front of a pool of identical servers.

blocks.text: 19.2 Watch position: a concrete eventual consistency example
blocks.content: 19.2 Watch position: a concrete eventual consistency example
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208157370-149681972.png
blocks.alt: When two devices update the same watch position at nearly the same time, the store resolves the conflict by keeping whichever write has the newer timestamp

blocks.text: This is the cleanest real example in the whole design. Suppose Alice is watching on her phone and also has the same title open, paused, on her television from earlier. Both devices might send a heartbeat within moments of each other. There is no need, and no time, for these two writes to coordinate strictly, the system simply keeps whichever write carries the newer client timestamp and lets the other one be silently overwritten. Occasionally that means a device resumes a few seconds off from exactly where a viewer expects, an outcome nobody has ever complained about, and a dramatically better trade than making every heartbeat wait on a distributed lock.

https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229325255-1966404.png
blocks.alt: A phone sends a heartbeat that gets stored, a TV later reads that position to resume and then overwrites it with a newer one, and a stale delayed heartbeat from the phone is correctly ignored because its timestamp is older

blocks.text: Trace it through concretely: the phone's heartbeat at 12 minutes 30 seconds gets stored with timestamp T1. Later, the TV opens the same title, reads that stored position back, and resumes from it. As the TV keeps playing it sends its own heartbeat at 25 minutes 10 seconds with a newer timestamp T2, which simply overwrites the earlier value. If a delayed, stale heartbeat from the phone then arrives carrying an older timestamp than T2, the store compares timestamps and discards it rather than accidentally rewinding Alice's progress. Last write wins, by timestamp, not by arrival order, is the entire consistency model this service needs.

20.2 Video durability

blocks.text: Once a rendition is written to origin storage, it needs to survive essentially forever, losing an encoded rendition would mean redoing real compute work and, worse, a temporary gap in what a title can offer. CDN edge caches, by deliberate contrast, need no such durability guarantee at all, they are disposable by design, a lost edge node loses nothing permanently, it just means the next request for that content is a cache miss that gets repopulated from a higher tier.

24.2 CDN push versus pull caching
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208191368-545228898.png
blocks.alt: Popular content can be proactively pushed to edge caches ahead of demand, while less predictable content is simply pulled and cached lazily on first request

blocks.text: Push, proactively prewarming edges for content expected to be popular, trades extra upfront bandwidth and coordination for guaranteeing the very first viewer gets a cache hit, which matters enormously for a coordinated release, per Section 26. Pull, caching lazily the first time any edge actually sees a request for something, is simpler and wastes no bandwidth on content that might never actually be requested in a given ISP's footprint. This design leans on push specifically for anticipated high demand titles and pull for everything else, which is the same 80/20 instinct behind most caching systems, spend the extra effort where it clearly pays off and let the simpler default handle the long tail.

blocks.title: Why retries are bounded, not infinite
blocks.text: A worker crash or a transient storage hiccup should not permanently block a title from becoming available, so a failed job is retried automatically. But an endlessly retried job that is failing for a real reason, a corrupt source chunk, for instance, would silently loop forever and never surface to anyone. Capping attempts and routing exhausted jobs to a dead letter queue turns a silent infinite loop into a visible signal a human can act on.

class CdnEdgeCacheClient:
    """A small illustrative stand-in for an ISP edge cache appliance: a bounded
    LRU cache of segment bytes that falls back to a slower upstream on a miss,
    then populates itself for next time."""

    def __init__(self, capacity, upstream_fetch):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.upstream_fetch = upstream_fetch  # callable: segment_key -> bytes
        self.cache = OrderedDict()  # ordered so we can evict the least recently used

    def fetch_segment(self, segment_key):
        if segment_key in self.cache:
            self.cache.move_to_end(segment_key)  # mark as most recently used
            return self.cache[segment_key]  # cache hit, no upstream trip

        fetched = self.upstream_fetch(segment_key)  # cache miss, pull from regional or origin
        self.cache[segment_key] = fetched
        if len(self.cache) > self.capacity:
            self.cache.popitem(last=False)  # evict least recently used
        return fetched

blocks.title: Why an edge cache needs no durability guarantee
blocks.text: Notice this class never worries about persisting its cache to disk safely or surviving a crash. That is deliberate, per Section 20.2: an edge cache losing its contents loses nothing that cannot be re-fetched from upstream a moment later. That is precisely what makes it safe to run CDN edge caches as disposable, replaceable infrastructure rather than durable stores.
